claim: The byte a page prints `Small/BltIn/2-Stk/3-Stk` against is one table of four fixed responses, written once and reached from more than one place, and it sits after the drive stage rather than shaping what goes into it. One table, because an entry read on a type that is nothing but a drive stage and the same entry read from inside a pair land a median 0.18 dB apart across a hundred and thirteen twelfth-octave bands, where the same reading puts two different entries of the table 1.96 dB apart or more -- so the reading separates the entries by better than an order of magnitude over what it says separates these. After the drive stage, because the pair was read once with each of the two drive characters its selector offers, and those characters put out measurably different spectra: a median 3.87 dB apart in shape and 9.99 dB at their widest, one carrying nine decibels more above eight kilohertz and the other seven more through the midrange. A filter shaping the input to a nonlinearity does not divide out of the result, because the nonlinearity remaps whatever spectrum it is given; a filter after one does, exactly. The ratio between two amp entries is 0.09 dB apart between the two characters, which is under the runs' own repeats -- so it divides out, and the filter is on the output. The switch beside the byte is what puts the table in the path at all: at Off the profile is its own reference to a median of a seventh of a decibel, and at On it is a bandpass, 10.7 dB down through the bottom octave and 3.2 down above eight kilohertz against 4.9 up through the two to four kilohertz octave. Read in five more places the table holds and in a sixth it does not. The bass multi-effect is the one place that does not reach it. Driving the stage at 4 and at 127 rather than the 48 the first run held moves each entry's response by a median 0.165 and 0.18 dB -- a thirty-two-fold change in the drive byte, against a reading that puts two entries of the table 2.3 dB apart. The two families the first run could not reach return the same four as well: the stage followed by a chorus at 0.2 dB and the same stage as one of five in a guitar chain at 0.22, both at the same three entries and on the same band set. So one table is reached from three families, two printed shapes, at three different parameter numbers, and at three drive amounts spanning almost the whole byte. The bass multi is the exception and it is not a close one: its first three entries sit a median 7.7 dB from the same three read anywhere else, which is wider than the table's own entries are from each other, and its fourth setting -- the one its row prints no name against -- returns its reference to 0.13 dB while sitting 7.81 dB from the entry below it. Not the third entry repeated, not the fourth the other rows return, and not refused: the first entry, which is what the byte would give if its top value did not reach the table. The bass type was then asked which side of its own drive stage it sits on. Its own table sits after its own stage, so this unit has two of them and not one. Its entries move by a median 0.13 dB when the drive byte goes to 4 and 0.24 when it goes to 127, against its own entries sitting 6.41 dB from each other -- 27 times the larger of the two. So the one type that reaches different curves reaches them the same way the other five do, and the reading that would have made the disagreement an artefact of where the filter sits is refused. What is left is the plainest arrangement and not the cheapest one: two tables, one of four responses for the guitar-side types and one for the bass, each written after the nonlinearity it is heard through.
named: a fixed cabinet response, one short filter per entry, multiplying the drive stage's output
adds: The records say four settings of one byte return four band profiles, on each of four chains. What is read out of them here is that the four profiles are the same four wherever the byte is reached from, and that the filter multiplies the drive stage's output instead of feeding it -- neither of which is in any one record, because both are a comparison between records and one of them is a comparison between two different nonlinearities.
refutedBy: An entry read in a fourth place returning a profile that is not the one the other three return, by more than the spacing between two entries of the table. Or the ratio between two entries moving with the drive byte, which would put the filter before the nonlinearity after all and make the four profiles a reading of one drive amount rather than a table. Or the switch turning out to do something other than put the filter in the path -- if its Off position were a fifth response rather than no response, the whole reading of entry 0 as a narrow box would go with it.
whatItWouldChange: Sixteen of sixty-four types stop needing their own cabinet stage. One filter bank of four fixed responses, a switch, and a byte that picks an index, serves every one of them.

The order inside a drive stage is fixed: drive, then the cabinet. A renderer that put the cabinet first would be wrong by the whole difference between two drive characters, which this unit shows is up to ten decibels of spectrum.

A renderer needs two cabinet tables and not one, and which of them a type reaches is decided by the type rather than by the byte -- the same four names index different responses on the bass multi than everywhere else.

eraPriors.claim: A cabinet response on a fixed-point part of this period is a short fixed filter, and its entries are expensive: each is a set of coefficients rather than a number. A table four entries long is what an expensive entry looks like, and it is the reason there is no continuous control beside it -- the same reasoning that makes a frequency table sixteen entries long and a gain table a hundred and twenty-eight.
eraPriors.why: It says why four, and why the four are reached by a byte with four values rather than swept. It carries nothing about where in the chain the filter sits, which is the part the measurement settled.
eraPriors.wouldBeWrongIf: The byte had accepted more than four values, or the response had moved continuously with it. The run asked all four printed entries and the reading separates them; a fifth was not asked and is named below as something this does not settle.

alternatives.reading: The four names are four names. Each type carries its own responses and they happen to be printed the same.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: The entries read in two places land a median 0.18 dB apart or closer, where the same reading puts two different entries 1.96 dB apart or further. Four records, three types, two of which are not the same kind of type at all.

alternatives.reading: The filter shapes what goes into the drive stage rather than what comes out of it, which is what a real amplifier's tone stack does on one side of the valve.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: The two drive characters. A filter before a nonlinearity cannot divide out of the result, because the nonlinearity is handed a different spectrum at each entry; these two characters differ by a median 3.87 dB and 9.99 dB at their widest, and the ratio between amp entries is the same across both to 0.09 dB.

alternatives.reading: The response is fixed against which nonlinearity precedes it and not against how hard that nonlinearity is driven, so the table is four curves at one drive amount and something else at another.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: The same sweep at a drive of 4 and at a drive of 127. Each entry's response moved by a median 0.165 and 0.18 dB against the 48 the first run held, on a reading that separates two entries of the table by 2.3 dB -- 13.9 and 12.8 times larger. The drive byte spans almost its whole range between those two and the table does not follow it.

separatedBy.observable: The same sweep of `01 10 / 40 03 04` at two more drive amounts, one near nought and one at full, read on the same band set. Each entry's profile against entry 0 either is the profile it was at 48 or it is not.

predicts.a fixed response after the stage: The same three profiles at all three drive amounts, to within the run's own repeats. A filter on the output does not know how hard the stage ahead of it was driven.
predicts.a response that moves with the drive byt: Profiles that move between drive amounts. How far is not predicted and does not need to be: anything clearing the repeats is an answer, because the claim says the figure is zero.

separatedBy.divergence: 2.2 dB, the closest two entries of the table come to each other under this reading, taken as what a difference worth having would be.
separatedBy.sensitivity_here: 0.42 dB, the median of the run's own repeat spread across the band set on the record this would repeat.

alternatives.reading: The twelve types that print this byte and were not read reach some other table. Upheld for one of them and refused for two: this is recorded as the reading it turned out to be rather than as one that fell.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: Answered rather than refuted, and it split. The two guitar-side families read -- the stage followed by a chorus and the stage inside a guitar chain -- return the same four curves as the standalone type, a median 0.2 and 0.22 dB apart. The bass multi does not, at 7.7 dB. So there is a second table on this unit and it is on the one type whose printed row is short, which is the place a second table was least surprising and was still worth measuring rather than assuming.

A response in front of the stage does not survive a thirty-two-fold change in how hard that stage is driven; this one does not notice it.
